items.plain: If friends die far away, they have only met the common fate of mortals. You cannot wish to live to old age and also never see anyone you love die.
items.core_idea: Living long means seeing loved ones die

items.plain: Remind yourself that anyone you love is mortal and not truly yours; they are given for a season, like a fig. Wanting your child or friend when that is not allowed is wanting a fig in winter.
items.core_idea: Loved ones are lent for a season, not owned

items.plain: Calling death a bad omen is like calling falling leaves or ripening grapes one. These are changes, not destruction; death is a larger change, into something that does not yet exist.
items.core_idea: Death is a change of state, not destruction

items.plain: It is a strong thing to be able to say: I knew my son was mortal. Likewise say: I knew I am mortal, and could lose my home or be imprisoned.
items.core_idea: Expect loss, and it will not surprise you

items.plain: If you have given up the struggle for a good life, you can start again at once, without waiting. Each time you give up you can renew it, and one victory makes you like one who never quit.
items.core_idea: You can always begin the struggle again

items.plain: Can something be shameful to you that you did not do or cause, like a fever? If your parents were poor or left their property to others, is that your shame?
items.core_idea: You are not shamed by what you did not do

items.plain: Why grieve? Fear comes from what you expect, and grief from what is already present.
items.core_idea: Fear looks ahead; grief comes from the present

items.plain: Do not stay so close to old friends that you sink to their habits, or you will ruin yourself. Changing has a cost: you must choose between being loved as before and being better but not treated the same.
items.core_idea: Growing may cost you old friendships

items.plain: When you lose something external, ask what you gained in its place. If it is worth more, such as calm or modesty instead of money or idle talk, do not call it a loss.
items.core_idea: Count what you gain, not only what you lose

items.plain: Not only the desire for power and riches makes us servile, but also the desire for calm, leisure, travel or learning. Whatever outside thing we prize puts us under others' control.
items.core_idea: Valuing any external thing makes you dependent

items.plain: If you have lessened your bad temper, harsh words, haste or laziness, you can celebrate every day for each good act. That is a greater reason for celebration than high office.
items.core_idea: Daily self-improvement is worth celebrating

items.plain: A neighbour throws stones and breaks your things; you did nothing wrong, and you are not an object but a free will. Only a wolf bites back; look at the human faculties you were given instead of revenge.
items.core_idea: Answer injury as a human, not a beast

items.plain: Afraid of being despised? Those who know you will not despise someone gentle and modest. As for those who do not know you, why care? No craftsman minds the opinion of people ignorant of his craft.
items.core_idea: Ignore the opinion of those who don't know you

items.plain: Another person's opinion of you is outside your will, so it is nothing to you. If it still upsets you, you have not really grasped what is good and evil.
items.core_idea: Others' opinions of you are not your concern

items.plain: Poverty, power or exile: I can bear any of them well. I was well not because of a place but because of my opinions, which no one can take from me, and with them I am content anywhere.
items.core_idea: Contentment comes from your opinions, not your place

items.plain: When you see someone powerful or rich, consider what you have instead. If you do not crave power or riches, you possess more than they do and something worth far more.
items.core_idea: Not wanting riches is worth more than riches

items.plain: All human troubles are about external things. What shall I do? How will it turn out? These are the words of people fixed on things outside the power of their will.
items.core_idea: Anxiety comes from fixing on what you can't control

items.plain: What would you like to be doing when death finds you? I would want to be doing something worthy of a human being: kind, useful to all, noble.
items.core_idea: Be found doing something good when death comes

items.plain: A prayer to God: thank you for the life you gave; I am content to have used what is yours. Take it back and place it where you choose, for everything was yours.
items.core_idea: Give back your life to God with thanks

items.plain: If you relax your attention for a while, do not think you can recover it at will. Each lapse builds a habit of inattention and of putting it off, and so you keep pushing away a good life.
items.core_idea: Lapses in attention become habits

items.plain: Saying 'Tomorrow I will pay attention' means 'Today I will be shameless, petty and passionate.' If attention is good tomorrow, it is better today, so you can keep it tomorrow too.
items.core_idea: Don't put off self-attention until tomorrow

items.plain: Some things are in our power, such as opinion, desire and aversion; others are not, such as body, property and reputation. Treat only what is yours as yours, and no one can compel or harm you.
items.core_idea: Control only what is yours; let the rest go

items.plain: Practise saying to every harsh impression: you are only an impression, not what you seem. Test it: if it concerns something not in your power, be ready to say it does not concern you.
items.core_idea: Test harsh impressions; ignore what you can't control

items.plain: With anything you love, remember what it really is. If you love a jug, know it is a jug, and its breaking won't upset you; when you kiss your child or wife, know you kiss a mortal.
items.core_idea: Remember the nature of what you love

items.plain: People are disturbed not by events but by their opinions about them; death is not terrible, the opinion that it is terrible is. So blame neither others nor ultimately yourself, but your opinions.
items.core_idea: Opinions, not events, disturb us

items.plain: Like a passenger ashore gathering shells, you may take up a wife and child, but keep listening for the captain. When he calls, leave everything and run to the ship; if you are old, stay close to it.
items.core_idea: Hold life's gifts loosely; be ready to leave

items.plain: Do not try to make things happen as you wish; wish them to happen as they do, and your life will flow calmly.
items.core_idea: Want things as they are, and find peace

items.plain: Illness hinders the body but not the will, unless the will chooses. Lameness hinders the leg, not the will. Whatever happens hinders something else, not you yourself.
items.core_idea: Hardship hinders the body, not the will

items.plain: Whenever something happens, ask what power you have to use it. Against attraction you have self-control, against pain endurance, against insults patience. Trained this way, impressions will not sweep you along.
items.core_idea: Every event calls on a strength you have

items.plain: Never say you lost something; say you gave it back, even a child, wife or estate. It doesn't matter through whom the giver took it back. While you have it, care for it like a traveller at an inn.
items.core_idea: Nothing is lost, only returned

items.plain: To improve, accept being thought foolish about external things, and distrust yourself if people think you important. You cannot both keep your will in line with nature and secure externals; caring for one neglects the other.
items.core_idea: Progress means letting others think you foolish

items.plain: If you want your children, wife and friends to live forever, you are foolish: you want what is not in your power to be in your power, and what belongs to others to be yours.
items.core_idea: Wanting loved ones to live forever is folly

items.plain: Act in life as at a banquet: take your share politely when a dish reaches you, do not hold it back as it passes, and do not reach for it early. Treat children, wife, office and wealth this way.
items.core_idea: Take life's gifts like dishes at a banquet

items.plain: When you see someone grieving a loss, do not be swept along as if outside things truly hurt him; it is his opinion that afflicts him. Show sympathy in words, even lament with him, but do not grieve inwardly.
items.core_idea: Sympathise outwardly without grieving inwardly

items.plain: You are an actor in a play the author chooses, short or long. Whether you play a poor man, a lame man or a ruler, your job is to play it well; choosing the part belongs to another.
items.core_idea: Play well the part you are given

items.plain: You can be unbeatable if you enter only contests you can win. Do not assume the powerful or honoured are happy; if the good lies in our power, there is no room for envy.
items.core_idea: Enter only contests you control, and envy fades

items.plain: It is not the person who insults or strikes you who wrongs you, but your opinion that it is insulting. When someone irritates you, your own opinion did it; pause, and you will master yourself more easily.
items.core_idea: Your opinion, not the insult, upsets you

items.plain: Keep death, exile and every dreadful thing, above all death, daily before your eyes, and you will never think meanly or crave anything too much.
items.core_idea: Remembering death keeps desires in check

items.plain: If you want philosophy, expect mockery. Don't look down on people, but hold to what seems best, as if posted there by God. Stay firm and mockers will later admire you; give in and be mocked twice.
items.core_idea: Expect ridicule, hold your principles, stay humble

items.plain: If you ever turn to outward things to please someone, you have lost your purpose. Be content to be a philosopher; if you want to seem one, seem so to yourself.
items.core_idea: Seek your own approval, not others'

items.plain: Do not worry about living without honour as a nobody. Office and invitations are not your business, so lacking them is no dishonour; be somebody in what is in your power, where you can be of great worth.
items.core_idea: Be somebody in what is in your power

items.plain: If someone is preferred over you at a dinner or in greetings, rejoice for him if these things are good; if they are bad, do not grieve at missing them.
items.core_idea: Don't grieve when others are preferred

items.plain: When a neighbour's cup breaks, we say such things happen; think the same when yours breaks. We call another's bereavement part of life, yet cry out at our own; remember how we view others' losses.
items.core_idea: Judge your losses as you judge others'

items.plain: You would be angry if someone handed your body over to any passer-by. Aren't you ashamed to hand your mind to anyone you meet, so that their insults disturb it?
items.core_idea: Don't let others' insults control your mind

items.plain: Before any act, consider what comes before it and what follows. Otherwise you will start eagerly without thinking ahead, and later, when ugly consequences appear, you will be ashamed.
items.core_idea: Think through consequences before you act

items.plain: If a brother wrongs you, keep your own stance towards him; ask not what he does but what you must do to keep your will in line with nature. No one damages you unless you think you are damaged.
items.core_idea: You are harmed only if you think so

items.plain: Set yourself at once a character and a way of being, and keep to it both when you are alone and when you are with people.
items.core_idea: Decide who you are, alone and in company

items.plain: If you hear someone speaks ill of you, do not defend yourself; reply that he did not know your other faults, or he would have mentioned more than these.
items.core_idea: Answer criticism by admitting more faults

items.plain: When visiting powerful people, expect to be turned away or ignored. If it is your duty to go anyway, bear what happens and never say it was not worth it; that is the mark of someone upset by externals.
items.core_idea: Expect rejection, do your duty anyway

items.plain: When a pleasure tempts you, pause and let it wait. Picture both the enjoyment and the regret afterwards, and how glad you will be if you abstain. If you do go ahead, don't let its charm conquer you.
items.core_idea: Pause before pleasure and weigh the aftermath

items.plain: Once you have decided something should be done, do not hide while doing it, even if many will disapprove. If it is wrong, don't do it; if it is right, why fear those who wrongly criticise?
items.core_idea: Do what is right openly, despite critics

items.plain: If you take on a role beyond your strength, you act badly in it and neglect the role you could have filled.
items.core_idea: Take on only the roles you can fulfil

items.plain: The body is the measure of what you should own, as the foot is of the shoe. Keep to it and you stay within limits; pass it and there is no stopping, as a shoe becomes gilded, dyed, embroidered.
items.core_idea: Your needs set the limit for possessions

items.plain: Someone who treats you badly or speaks ill of you does what seems right to him. If he is mistaken, he is the one harmed, because he is deceived. So be gentle, and say: it seemed so to him.
items.core_idea: Those who wrong you hurt themselves; be gentle

items.plain: Everything has two handles, one you can carry it by and one you cannot. If your brother wrongs you, do not grab the wrong; grab the fact that he is your brother, raised with you, and you can bear it.
items.core_idea: Hold hard things by the handle you can bear

items.plain: Being richer or more eloquent than you does not make me better than you; it only means I have more property or better speech. But a person is neither property nor speech.
items.core_idea: Wealth or eloquence doesn't make you better

items.plain: If someone bathes quickly, say he bathes quickly, not badly; if he drinks a lot, say he drinks a lot. Until you know his reasons, how can you know he is doing wrong?
items.core_idea: Describe what people do; don't judge it

items.plain: Never call yourself a philosopher or lecture ordinary people on principles; act on them instead. At a dinner, do not say how people should eat; eat as you should.
items.core_idea: Live your principles instead of preaching them

items.plain: The untaught expect help and harm from outside; the philosopher expects them from himself. One making progress blames and praises no one, claims nothing, ignores praise and criticism, curbs desire, and watches himself like an enemy.
items.core_idea: Progress means looking to yourself, not outside

items.plain: You are an adult now. Keep postponing self-improvement and you will stay ignorant until you die. Live now as someone making progress; every trial is the contest, it cannot wait, and one surrender can undo progress.
items.core_idea: The time to improve is now, not later

items.plain: A prayer to Zeus and Destiny: lead me where I must go, and I will follow willingly; if I refuse, I make myself miserable and must follow anyway. Whoever yields nobly to necessity is wise in divine things.
items.core_idea: Follow fate willingly rather than be dragged

items.plain: Some things are in our power, like opinion, aim, desire and aversion; others are not, like body, property and reputation. Treat only what is yours as yours, and no one can compel or hurt you.
items.core_idea: Control only what is yours; let the rest go

items.plain: People are disturbed not by things but by their views of them; death is not terrible, the notion that it is terrible is. So blame not others but your own views; the wise blame neither others nor themselves.
items.core_idea: Our views, not things, disturb us

items.plain: Do not demand that events happen as you wish; wish them to happen as they do, and you will do well.
items.core_idea: Want things as they happen, and fare well

items.plain: Sickness hinders the body, but not the will unless it chooses. Lameness hinders the leg, not the will. Say this about everything that happens: it hinders something else, not truly you.
items.core_idea: Hardship hinders the body, not the will

items.plain: Whenever something happens, ask yourself what strength you have to use for it: self-control for attraction, endurance for pain, patience for insult. With this habit, events will not overwhelm you.
items.core_idea: Every event calls on a strength you have

items.plain: Never say you lost something; say you gave it back, even a child, wife or estate. It doesn't matter through whom the giver took it back. While you have it, treat it as not yours, like travellers at an inn.
items.core_idea: Nothing is lost, only returned

items.plain: To improve, be willing to be thought foolish about external things, and do not want to seem knowledgeable. If others think you important, distrust yourself; you cannot both keep your will in harmony with nature and secure externals.
items.core_idea: Progress means letting others think you foolish

items.plain: Behave in life as at a banquet: take a modest share when a dish reaches you, don't stop it as it passes, and don't long for it before it comes. Treat children, spouse, office and riches this way.
items.core_idea: Take life's gifts like dishes at a banquet

items.plain: When you see someone weeping over a loss, do not be overcome; what hurts him is not the event but the view he takes of it. Talk with him kindly, even groan with him, but do not groan inwardly.
items.core_idea: Sympathise outwardly without grieving inwardly

items.plain: You are an actor in a play the Author chooses, short or long. Whether you play a poor man, a cripple or a ruler, act it well; that is your job, but choosing the part belongs to another.
items.core_idea: Play well the part you are given

items.plain: You can be unconquerable if you fight only battles you can win. Do not assume the honoured or powerful are happy; if good lies in what is in our power, there is no room for envy. Seek freedom, not rank.
items.core_idea: Fight only battles you control; seek freedom

items.plain: It is not the person who abuses or strikes you who insults you, but your view that it is insulting. When provoked, know that your own opinion provokes you; take time before reacting and you will control yourself.
items.core_idea: Your view, not the insult, provokes you

items.plain: If you want philosophy, expect to be laughed at. Don't look superior, but hold to what seems best as one placed there by God. Persist, and the mockers will later admire you; give in, and you will be mocked twice.
items.core_idea: Expect ridicule, hold your principles, stay humble

items.plain: Do not worry that you will live in discredit and be nobody. Power and invitations are not your business, so missing them is no disgrace; be somebody in what lies in your power, where you can matter most.
items.core_idea: Be somebody in what is in your power

items.plain: If someone is preferred before you at a party or in courtesies, rejoice for him if these things are good; if they are bad, do not grieve that you lack them.
items.core_idea: Don't grieve when others are preferred

items.plain: You would be angry if someone handed your body over to a stranger. Aren't you ashamed to hand your mind to anyone who insults you, to be upset and confused?
items.core_idea: Don't let insults take over your mind

items.plain: In everything, consider what comes before and after, then begin. Otherwise you will start with energy, careless of consequences, and quit in shame when they appear.
items.core_idea: Think through consequences before you begin

items.plain: If a brother is unjust, keep your own just stance towards him. Think not of what he does but of keeping your will in line with nature; you are hurt only when you consent to be hurt.
items.core_idea: You are hurt only if you consent

items.plain: If someone tells you a person speaks ill of you, do not make excuses; say he must not know your other faults, or he would have mentioned more.
items.core_idea: Answer criticism by admitting more faults

items.plain: When a promised pleasure dazzles you, don't be swept away; make it wait. Picture both the enjoyment and the regret afterwards, against the pride of abstaining. Even if it seems fitting, don't let its lure conquer you.
items.core_idea: Pause before pleasure and weigh the aftermath

items.plain: When you have clearly judged something should be done, never shrink from being seen doing it, even if people misunderstand. If it is wrong, don't do it; if it is right, why fear unfair critics?
items.core_idea: Do what is right openly, despite critics

items.plain: If you take on a role beyond your strength, you handle it badly and give up a role you could have carried.
items.core_idea: Take on only the roles you can carry

items.plain: Someone who harms you or speaks ill of you follows what seems right to him, not to you. If he is mistaken, he is the one hurt, since he is deceived. So bear him gently: it seemed so to him.
items.core_idea: Those who wrong you hurt themselves; be gentle

items.plain: Everything has two handles: one you can carry it by and one you cannot. If your brother wrongs you, don't take hold of his wrong; take hold of the fact that he is your brother, raised with you.
items.core_idea: Hold hard things by the handle you can bear

items.plain: Being richer or more eloquent does not make me your superior; it only means my possessions or style exceed yours. And you are neither your property nor your style.
items.core_idea: Wealth or eloquence doesn't make you superior

items.plain: How long will you put off demanding the best of yourself? You know the principles and are no longer a boy. Keep postponing and you will stay ordinary until death. From now on, live as a mature, progressing person.
items.core_idea: Stop delaying; start living wisely now

items.plain: A prayer to Zeus and Destiny: lead me wherever my lot is fixed, and I follow cheerfully. If I refused, I would be wicked and miserable and still have to follow.
items.core_idea: Follow fate cheerfully; you must follow anyway

items.plain: You go ahead of yourself: everything you have built is only the base for a greater self, and that self in turn will be a base for more.
items.core_idea: You are always building toward a larger self

items.plain: We have always gone ahead of ourselves and always will. All we gather is only seed for fields not yet ploughed; we are both the fields and the ploughmen, the harvesters and the harvest.
items.core_idea: We are both the sowers and the harvest

items.plain: A prayer to love, which has given my desires dignity: let my stronger self not take what tempts my weaker self. I would rather starve and die than reach for a cup love did not fill or bless.
items.core_idea: Take only what love has blessed

items.plain: Many give up a kingdom for solitude, and eagles come down among moles to learn the earth's secrets. Some give up dreams to stay near the dreamless, or cover their souls so others aren't shamed by naked truth.
items.core_idea: People give up great things to stay close to others

items.plain: On an island I saw a monster endlessly eating earth and drinking sea. I asked if he was never satisfied. He said he was full, even weary of it, but afraid there would be nothing left tomorrow.
items.core_idea: Fear of tomorrow drives endless craving

items.plain: Two eagles circling over a lamb began fighting each other. The astonished sheep told her lamb the sky was large enough for both, and to pray that God make peace between his winged brothers. The lamb prayed.
items.core_idea: The innocent pray even for their predators

items.plain: The astonished traveller cried that since his horse was stolen, everyone had rushed to list his faults, yet no one said a word against the thief.
items.core_idea: People blame the victim, not the wrongdoer

items.plain: The weather-cock complained to the wind that it was dull and always blew in its face, disturbing the stability God gave it. The wind did not answer; it only laughed in space.
items.core_idea: The vain blame the world for their own position

items.plain: A bird rose from deep in my heart and flew upward, growing as it rose, from a swallow to something that filled the heavens. Yet it never left my heart.
items.core_idea: What rises from the heart still stays within it

items.plain: My faith, how can I rise to your height? I am chained like a prisoner who cannot see the temple's domes, and cannot fly with you. Yet you rise from my heart, my heart holds you, and I am content.
items.core_idea: Faith soars beyond me, yet lives in my heart

items.plain: A white sheet of paper vowed to stay pure forever and never let ink or dark touch it. The ink and the coloured pencils kept away. The paper did stay pure and chaste forever, and empty.
items.core_idea: Purity kept at all costs can leave life empty

items.plain: A man sold a beautiful statue he had dug up to a collector. Walking home, he wondered how anyone could pay so much for dead stone. The collector wondered how anyone could trade such life for dead money.
items.core_idea: Each values what the other thinks is dead

items.plain: One fish told another there is a sea above theirs where creatures live as they do. The other scoffed: anything that leaves our sea dies, so what proof is there of life in other seas?
items.core_idea: We doubt any life beyond what we know

items.plain: On a dark night a man stole his neighbour's biggest melon. When he opened it at home and found it unripe, his conscience suddenly woke, and he regretted the theft.
items.core_idea: Conscience often wakes only when the gain fails

items.plain: The wish to die, though stronger than anything, is held back by a wish to live that is weaker than anything.
items.core_idea: A faint will to live can hold back despair

items.plain: Memory holds my spirit here: a line of distant days, a youth spent dreaming, a face, a voice that lingers, a hand touching mine.
items.core_idea: Memories of love hold the spirit back

items.plain: Beyond my solitude is a deeper one, to whose dweller my aloneness seems a crowded market and my silence noise. I am too young and restless to seek it; the world's voices and shadows still hold me back.
items.core_idea: There is always a deeper solitude beyond yours

items.plain: Beyond my burdened self lives a freer self, but I am too young and angry to be it. How can I be free unless my burdened selves die, or all people are free, or my roots wither and fledglings leave?
items.core_idea: Freedom requires letting go of what holds you

items.plain: You want love in a cup, not as a rushing river. You listen to its faint murmur, but when love shouts you cover your ears.
items.core_idea: We want love only in small, safe amounts

items.plain: Night is ending, and we children of night must die at dawn; from our ashes a stronger love will rise, laughing in the sun and never dying.
items.core_idea: From our ending a deathless love will rise

items.plain: In my madness I found freedom and safety: the freedom of being alone, and safety from being understood, since those who understand us enslave part of us. Yet a jailed thief is also safe from thieves.
items.core_idea: Being understood can enslave part of you

items.plain: For thousands of years I called myself God's slave, creation and son, and God passed by in silence. When I said we grow together, his root and his flower, God enfolded me, and was in the valleys too.
items.core_idea: God answers when we see ourselves as one with him

items.plain: Friend, I am not what I seem; appearance is a garment that shields me from your questions and you from my neglect. My true self lives in silence, forever unseen and unreachable.
items.core_idea: The true self stays hidden behind appearances

items.plain: Friend, you are not my friend, but how can I make you understand? My path is not yours, yet we walk together hand in hand.
items.core_idea: We walk together on different paths

items.plain: A scarecrow said he never tired of the joy of scaring; I said I knew it too. He replied only those stuffed with straw know it; praise or insult? A year later, crows nested under his hat.
items.core_idea: Those who frighten others are hollow in the end

items.plain: A mother and daughter, sleepwalking, met in their garden and poured out their hatred: each blamed the other for ruining her life. A cock crowed, they woke, and spoke to each other gently.
items.core_idea: Hidden resentments lie beneath polite affection

items.plain: A wise dog passed cats being told that if they prayed with faith it would rain mice. He laughed inwardly at the foolish cats: surely what rains down for prayer and faith is not mice but bones.
items.core_idea: Everyone imagines heaven serves their own appetite

items.plain: A man with a valley full of needles was asked by Jesus's mother for one, to mend her son's torn garment. He gave her no needle, only a learned lecture on giving and taking to take to her son.
items.core_idea: Talk about generosity is no substitute for giving

items.plain: Seeing his long shadow at sunrise, a fox decided he would eat a camel for lunch and hunted camels all morning. At noon he saw his shadow again and said a mouse will do.
items.core_idea: Ambitions shrink as the day goes on

items.plain: A witch poisoned the city well so all who drank went mad. Everyone drank except the king and his chamberlain, and the people said the king was mad. So he drank too, and the city rejoiced at his recovered reason.
items.core_idea: To the mad crowd, sanity looks like madness

items.plain: I invented a new pleasure, and as I tried it an angel and a devil rushed to my door and fought over it, one crying sin, the other virtue.
items.core_idea: The same pleasure is called sin and virtue

items.plain: In my father's garden are two cages, one with a lion from the desert and one with a sparrow that does not sing. Each dawn the sparrow greets the lion as a fellow prisoner.
items.core_idea: Great and small alike can be prisoners

items.plain: Three ants on a sleeping man's nose complained the land was barren. The third said they stood on the Supreme Ant, too vast to see or hear. The others laughed. Then the man scratched his nose and crushed them.
items.core_idea: We mock what is too vast for us to perceive

items.plain: As I buried one of my dead selves, the grave-digger said he liked only me: everyone else came and went weeping, while I came laughing and went laughing.
items.core_idea: Bury your old selves with laughter, not tears

items.plain: The Evil God complained to the Good God that people kept mistaking him for the Good God. The Good God said people mistook him for the Evil God too. The Evil God walked off cursing human stupidity.
items.core_idea: People confuse good and evil

items.plain: My defeat is dearer to me than a thousand triumphs. Through it I know myself and find joy in being scorned. It taught me that being enthroned is enslavement, and being understood is being levelled down.
items.core_idea: Defeat teaches more and frees more than triumph

items.plain: My defeat, my undying courage: together we will laugh with the storm, bury all that dies in us, stand firmly in the sun, and be dangerous.
items.core_idea: Defeat can become fearless courage

items.plain: I have seen faces with many expressions and one fixed one, shine hiding ugliness and shine hiding beauty, old faces lined with nothing and smooth ones engraved with everything. I know faces because I look beneath appearances.
items.core_idea: See past appearances to what lies beneath

items.plain: A friend called a blind man the wisest in the land. I asked the man, blind from birth, what wisdom he followed. He said he was an astronomer, and touching his chest, said he watches all these suns and stars.
items.core_idea: The universe can be seen within

items.plain: I sit between my brother the mountain and my sister the sea. We three are one in our loneliness, bound by a deep, strong and strange love.
items.core_idea: Loneliness can be a shared bond

items.plain: A blade of grass complained that a falling leaf was noisy; the leaf scorned it as lowly. The leaf fell asleep, came back in spring as grass, and in autumn grumbled that the falling leaves were so noisy.
items.core_idea: We condemn others, then become them

items.plain: The Eye saw a beautiful mountain in the mist. The Ear could not hear it, the Hand could not touch it, the Nose could not smell it. So they all agreed something must be wrong with the Eye.
items.core_idea: People dismiss what their own senses cannot perceive

items.plain: Two scholars, one an unbeliever and one a believer, argued for hours about the gods. That evening the unbeliever went to the temple and begged forgiveness, and the believer burned his sacred books, having become an unbeliever.
items.core_idea: Arguments can convert each side to the other

items.plain: My Sorrow died like all living things, leaving me alone to think. Now my words feel heavy, no one hears my songs or looks at me, and in sleep voices pity the man whose Sorrow is dead.
items.core_idea: Losing your sorrow can leave you unseen

items.plain: My Joy grew pale because no other heart shared it, and it died of isolation. Now I remember my dead Joy only with my dead Sorrow, but memory is an autumn leaf that murmurs briefly and falls silent.
items.core_idea: Joy unshared dies of isolation

items.plain: I live among a perfect race, the most imperfect one, a human chaos moving among finished worlds whose people have complete laws, pure order, and thoughts, dreams and visions all sorted and recorded.
items.core_idea: Feeling chaotic among people who seem perfect

items.plain: This is a perfect world, God's ripest fruit. So why am I here, O God, a green seed of unfulfilled passion, a directionless storm, a fragment of a burnt planet? Why, God of lost souls, yourself lost among gods?
items.core_idea: Asking God why a restless soul belongs here

items.plain: I walk forever along these shores between the sand and the foam. The tide will erase my footprints and the wind will blow the foam away, but the sea and shore will remain forever.
items.core_idea: Our traces fade; the sea and shore remain

items.plain: Only yesterday I thought I was a fragment trembling out of rhythm in life. Now I know I am the whole sphere, and all life moves within me in rhythmic fragments.
items.core_idea: You are not a fragment; life moves within you

items.plain: Awake, people tell me I and my world are a grain of sand on an infinite shore. In my dream I tell them I am the infinite sea, and all worlds are grains of sand on my shore.
items.core_idea: You are the sea, not the grain of sand

items.plain: Only once have I been left speechless: when someone asked me who I am.
items.core_idea: The hardest question is who you are

items.plain: A pearl is a temple that pain builds around a grain of sand. What longing built our bodies, and around what grains?
items.core_idea: Pain and longing build beautiful things

items.plain: When God threw me like a pebble into this wonderful lake, I stirred its surface with countless circles. But when I reached the depths, I became very still.
items.core_idea: Depth brings stillness after surface turmoil

items.plain: Give me silence, and I will be bolder than the night.
items.core_idea: Silence gives courage to face the dark

items.plain: I was born a second time when my soul and my body loved each other and became one.
items.core_idea: Soul and body united bring rebirth

items.plain: Remembering is a kind of meeting. Forgetting is a kind of freedom.
items.core_idea: Memory reunites; forgetting frees

items.plain: Don't the spirits living in the sky envy humans their pain?
items.core_idea: Pain may be a gift even spirits envy

items.plain: A pilgrim told me to follow him to the Holy City in a day and a night. We walked many days and nights without reaching it, and to my surprise he grew angry with me because he had misled me.
items.core_idea: Those who mislead us often blame us for it

items.plain: God, let me be the lion's prey before you let the rabbit be mine.
items.core_idea: Better to be prey than prey on the weak

items.plain: You can reach the dawn only by going through the night.
items.core_idea: Only through darkness do we reach the dawn

items.plain: My house begs me to stay with my past; the road calls me to my future. I tell them I have neither: in staying there is going, in going there is staying. Only love and death change everything.
items.core_idea: Only love and death truly change things

items.plain: How can I lose faith in life's fairness, when those who sleep on feathers dream no more beautifully than those who sleep on the bare ground?
items.core_idea: Dreams are equal for rich and poor

items.plain: Strangely, wanting certain pleasures is part of my pain.
items.core_idea: Desire itself can be a source of pain

items.plain: I have despised my soul seven times: when it was meek to rise, limped before the lame, chose the easy, excused its wrong by others', called weakness patience, scorned a face that was its own mask, and prized its praise-song.
items.core_idea: Seven ways the soul betrays itself

items.plain: I do not know absolute truth, but I am humble about my ignorance, and that humility is my honour and reward.
items.core_idea: Humility before ignorance is its own honour

items.plain: Between what we imagine and what we achieve lies a gap that only our longing can cross.
items.core_idea: Longing bridges imagination and achievement

items.plain: Paradise is just behind that door, in the next room, but I have lost the key. Maybe I have only misplaced it.
items.core_idea: Paradise is near; we've only mislaid the key

items.plain: You are blind and I cannot hear or speak, so let us touch hands and understand each other.
items.core_idea: Understanding can pass beyond words and sight

items.plain: A person's meaning lies not in what they achieve but in what they long to achieve.
items.core_idea: We are defined by our longings, not achievements

items.plain: Some of us are like ink and some like paper. Without the dark ones, some would have no voice; without the light ones, some could not see.
items.core_idea: We need each other's differences to be seen and heard

items.plain: If you listen to me, I will give you a voice.
items.core_idea: Listening is repaid with a voice

items.plain: Our mind is like a sponge and our heart like a stream. Isn't it strange that most of us choose to soak things up rather than to flow?
items.core_idea: Choose to flow like the heart, not absorb
